title: Homestay Villages Around Darjeeling Compared
meta_description: Lamahatta, Takdah, Tinchuley, Lepchajagat, Chatakpur and more: altitude, distance from Darjeeling, homestay rates and what to ask before you book.
summary: The villages within 20–35 km of Darjeeling offer quiet homestays at about ₹1,500–2,500 a person with dinner and breakfast. Lepchajagat and Chatakpur are high forest villages, Lamahatta, Takdah and Tinchuley sit among pines and tea on the Teesta side, and Mungpoo, Peshok and Bijanbari are lower and warmer. Here is how they compare.

sections.heading: Why stay in a village, not the town
paras: Darjeeling town is wonderful for two or three days: the Mall, the toy train, the bakeries, the mountaineering institute. But it is crowded, its roads jam at school times and in season, and a decent room near Chowrasta in October costs more than many visitors expect. Half an hour or an hour away, the picture changes. Families who farm, pluck tea or work in town have opened their houses to guests, and a night there costs about ₹1,500–2,500 a person with home-cooked dinner and breakfast.

What you get is quiet, a kitchen fire, food grown on the slope outside, and hosts who know which ridge the mountain shows above and when. What you give up is choice: one dinner menu, simple bathrooms, patchy network in places and a reliance on a car or shared jeep to get anywhere. For most of our travellers the trade is worth it, and the best trips we plan pair two or three nights in town with one or two in a village.

sections.heading: High and misty: Lepchajagat and Chatakpur
paras: Lepchajagat sits at about 2,100 m on the road from Ghoom to Sukhia Pokhari, roughly 19 km from Darjeeling. The name reads as the place or world of the Lepchas, the oldest people of these hills. It is a strip of homes along a forest of pine, oak and rhododendron, with a viewpoint for Kanchenjunga at dawn and mist that usually rolls in by afternoon. Birders like it; so do people who want to do nothing at all. Besides family homestays there is the WBFDC Lepchajagat Nature and Wilderness Resort, with six rooms booked on the forest corporation's portal, which opens 90 days ahead.

Chatakpur is higher still, around 2,400 m, inside the Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary. It is tiny, about 19 houses, and was developed as an eco-village with the villagers' forest committee; nearly every family hosts guests. The last 7 km is a rough forest track up from Sonada on the Hill Cart Road, so you need a reserved four-wheel drive. A confirmed booking is essential, and your host collects the forest entry fee. It is the quietest place in this guide and the coldest at night.

Close by, Jorepokhri's twin ponds near Sukhia Pokhari have the GTA Jorepokhri Tourist Lodge. The salamander sanctuary there no longer shows breeding newts after paving changed the ponds, so go for the lake walk and the tea of nearby Mim, not for wildlife.

sections.heading: Pines and orchards: Lamahatta, Takdah, Tinchuley
paras: These three lie on the Teesta side, below the Peshok road, and make an easy two-night circuit. Lamahatta, about 23 km from Darjeeling at roughly 1,700–1,750 m, is a village eco-tourism park opened around 2012: terraced gardens, tall dhupi trees, prayer flags and a 30–45 minute uphill trail to a small lake that villagers hold sacred. The name is read locally as the monks' settlement. Homestays sit on the slope around the park, and on clear mornings the mountains show over the trees.

Takdah, around 28 km out, was a British army cantonment in the early 1900s. Several of the old officers' bungalows still stand, some run as heritage homestays with wooden floors and fireplaces, and there is a government orchid centre that flowers best from February to April. Tinchuley, about 3 km on and a little higher, is the name for three hilltops said to look like clay ovens. It is a village of orange orchards and tea, with the Gumbadara viewpoint over the Teesta valley. Walk between the two in about an hour.

sections.heading: Low and warm: Peshok, Mungpoo, Bijanbari
paras: Drop below 1,200 m and the air changes: warmer winters, hotter wet summers, more birds, fewer jackets. Peshok, on the road from Ghoom down to Teesta Bazar, is tea country, with the Peshok and Lopchu estates and the viewpoint over the meeting of the Teesta and Rangeet. A handful of homestays and tea-garden stays sit along this road.

Mungpoo, around 33 km away, is a government cinchona plantation that has made quinine since 1864. Rabindranath Tagore stayed here four times between 1938 and 1940, and the house is now the Rabindra Museum. The village has only a few homestays, so book ahead around Tagore's birthday in early May. Bijanbari, about 35 km away by Pulbazar, lies at roughly 750–800 m in the Chhota Rangeet valley: maize, oranges and cardamom, and a road that continues toward Rimbik. Choose it in winter, when the high villages are cold.

sections.heading: What to ask before you book
paras: Most village homestays are booked by phone or WhatsApp, often through a relative in town. Photos online can be old, and a ten-minute call saves a cold, disappointing night. These are the questions we ask on behalf of our travellers.
list: Is the rate per person or per room, and does it include dinner, breakfast and evening tea?
Is the bathroom attached, with a Western toilet and a geyser, or is hot water a bucket on request?
Are there heavy quilts or a room heater in winter, and is there an inverter for power cuts?
Can a car reach the door, or is the last stretch a walk with luggage, and is it steep?
Which mobile network works, and is there Wi-Fi?
Which way does the room face, and can you see the mountains from it or only from a nearby viewpoint?
How much advance do you need, and what happens to it if a landslide blocks the road?
Can you arrange a pick-up from Darjeeling, Ghoom or the jeep stand, and at what price?
Is there anything you would like us to bring from town, and do you mind if we join you in the kitchen?

sections.heading: Government lodges and the honest costs
paras: If you prefer a booking with a receipt from an official portal, two government stays work well in this area. The WBFDC resort at Lepchajagat, mentioned above, is small and fills fast on long weekends. The GTA Jorepokhri Tourist Lodge sits by the twin lakes near Sukhia Pokhari. Both are plain and functional, and priced for Indian families rather than tourists with deep pockets. Rates and booking rules change, so check current status before you travel.

Budget for transport as well as beds. A shared jeep from Darjeeling to Sukhia Pokhari costs about ₹70–100 a seat, and to Ghoom ₹30–50, but most of these villages are off the jeep routes, so a reserved car for the day runs about ₹2,500–4,000. Two or three village nights in one loop, such as Lamahatta, Takdah and Tinchuley, share that cost well. Carry some cash: few homestays take cards and village ATMs are rare.

Be a good guest and the welcome grows. Tell your host your arrival time and any food needs a day ahead, since dinner is cooked fresh and supplies come from town. Eat what is served, at the time it is served. Switch off lights and geysers, take your plastic back to Darjeeling, and ask before photographing family members or the prayer room. A small gift from town, such as fruit or sweets for the children, is always welcome.

faqs.q: Which homestay village near Darjeeling is best for a first visit?
faqs.a: Lamahatta is the easiest first choice: about 23 km from Darjeeling on a good road, with a short lake trail, gardens and many homestays to compare. If you want forest and a dawn mountain view, choose Lepchajagat, about 19 km away. For a quieter two-night loop with old bungalows and orchards, pair Takdah and Tinchuley, about an hour's walk apart.

faqs.q: How much does a homestay near Darjeeling cost?
faqs.a: Expect about ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with dinner and breakfast in 2025–26, a little more in Chatakpur, where the forest entry fee is added, and in the Takdah heritage bungalows. Children usually pay less. Rates rise around the Puja holidays and New Year. Confirm whether the price is per person or per room before you pay any advance.

faqs.q: Can I reach these villages by shared jeep?
faqs.a: Some, yes. Shared jeeps run from Darjeeling to Ghoom (₹30–50) and Sukhia Pokhari (₹70–100), which puts Lepchajagat and Jorepokhri within easy reach, and jeeps on the Teesta road pass near Peshok. Lamahatta, Takdah, Tinchuley and Mungpoo have thinner services. Chatakpur needs a reserved four-wheel drive from Sonada. Most travellers hire a car for about ₹2,500–4,000 a day.

faqs.q: Is Chatakpur worth the rough road?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want true quiet. Chatakpur, at about 2,400 m inside the Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary, is a village of around 19 houses with forest on every side, birds at dawn and Kanchenjunga on clear mornings. The last 7 km from Sonada is a rough track for four-wheel drives. You must book ahead, and nights are cold, so pack warm clothes.

faqs.q: Which village near Darjeeling is warm in winter?
faqs.a: Bijanbari, at roughly 750–800 m in the Chhota Rangeet valley, is the warmest, with mild winter days. Peshok and Mungpoo, at about 1,000–1,200 m, are also noticeably warmer than Darjeeling. Lepchajagat, Jorepokhri and Chatakpur, all above 2,000 m, can drop near freezing from December to February, so ask about heavy quilts and heaters if you go then.

faqs.q: Are there government lodges in the villages around Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Yes, two that we suggest. The WBFDC Lepchajagat Nature and Wilderness Resort has six rooms, booked on the forest corporation's portal, which opens 90 days ahead. The GTA Jorepokhri Tourist Lodge sits by the twin lakes near Sukhia Pokhari. Both are simple and good value. Booking rules and rates change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from these homestays?
faqs.a: From many of them, on clear mornings between October and early December and in March and April. Lepchajagat, Chatakpur, Lamahatta and Tinchuley's Gumbadara viewpoint all face the range. Not every room has the view, so ask which way your window faces. From June to September cloud usually hides the mountains, though the forest and tea are at their greenest.

faqs.q: Do village homestays have hot water and Wi-Fi?
faqs.a: Most now have attached bathrooms, and many have geysers, but in some homes hot water still comes in a bucket on request. Mobile data works in most villages, with Jio and Airtel usually strongest, but signal fades in valleys and forest. Wi-Fi is less common. Power cuts happen in storms, so ask whether there is an inverter and carry a torch.

faqs.q: How many nights should I spend in a village near Darjeeling?
faqs.a: One night is enough for a taste, but two let you see a dawn, take a walk and actually rest. A good plan is two or three nights in Darjeeling town, then one or two in a village such as Lamahatta or Lepchajagat. For a loop of Lamahatta, Takdah and Tinchuley, allow two nights so you are not spending the whole trip in a car.
